stem: A 21-year-old man is dropped off at the ED by friends after being stabbed in the thigh. The patient's jeans are soaked with blood. On examination his vitals are as follows: HR - 137, BP - 76/38, RR - 24, O2 sat - 98% on room air, T - 37.3°C PO The nurse has placed the patient on a cardiorespiratory monitor, established 2 large bore IVs, and has given a 1 L bolus of Ringer's lactate. Despite application of a tourniquet and direct pressure, the wound keeps bleeding briskly. What is your next best step?

options.html: Give crossmatched packed cells when available
Give another 1L bolus of Ringer's lactate

answer: The correct answer is D. D; Airway and Breathing are satisfactory. There is no need to intubate. Circulation is not - this patient is in hemorrhagic shock. Aside from trying to prevent ongoing blood loss, you need to replace blood loss. Initially it is acceptable to use crystalloid to expand the intravascular space, but more than 1L is not recommended as crystalloid does not have oxygen carrying capacity. This patient has not responded adequately to the 1L bolus of Ringer's lactate and he is still bleeding. You should not wait for crossmatched packed cells, this takes too much time. This patient is very sick. You also should not await CBC results, as the Hb will not be reflective of acute blood loss, so should not guide management, and will only result in dangerous delays.

stem: A 30-year-old pregnant woman presents to the ED with abdominal pain and heavy vaginal bleeding. The gestational age is approximately 7 weeks according to her last menstrual period. Her vital signs are: HR - 129, BP - 75/34, RR - 22, T - 37.1°C, O2 sat - 99% on room air She is awake and speaking to you, and there are no signs of airway obstruction. Auscultation of the chest is clear, and heart sounds are normal. She looks unwell, her skin is pale and capillary refill is delayed. Palpation of the abdomen reveals significant left lower quadrant tenderness. The patient has been placed on a cardiorespiratory monitor by nursing staff. What is your best NEXT step in managing this patient?

options.html: Obtain 2 large bore peripheral IV lines
Perform a bedside ultrasound looking for intra-abdominal free fluid
Obtain a formal ultrasound looking for ectopic pregnancy

answer: The correct answer is A. A; This patient is in shock. There are no immediate concerns re: airway and breathing so no current role for intubation or provision of supplementary oxygen. There is a concern re: circulation. Establish 2 large bore peripheral IV lines and start fluid resuscitation ASAP. It is a reasonable step after that to perform a bedside ultrasound. You would only consider getting a formal ultrasound to look for ectopic pregnancy if the patient stabilized, and it was still needed after PoCUS. A formal ultrasound involves transferring the patient outside of the ED where it is difficult and dangerous to manage an unstable patient.

stem: A 56-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with retrosternal chest pain after shovelling snow. He has a sudden loss of consciousness while you are taking the history. You cannot detect a pulse. The monitor shows the attached. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate therapy?
answer: The correct answer is B. B; The monitor shows VT. There is no pulse. If the crash cart is ready to go, defibrillate immediately. Cardioversion is only for rhythms with a pulse. IV amiodarone would only be later in the arrest sequence if defibrillation was unsuccessful. There is no role for IV NTG in pulseless patients. While MI may the underlying cause for the cardiac arrest, thrombolysis is not part of the initial cardiac arrest sequence.

stem: A 71-year-old man presents to the ED with a complaint of dysuria, frequency and urgency. He also feels generally unwell with lethargy and nausea. His vitals are as follows: HR - 128, BP - 82/50, RR - 22, O2 sat 95% on room air, T 38.6°C PO A nurse has placed the patient on a cardiorespiratory monitor and established a large bore IV. Which of the following outlines the most appropriate next steps in management of this patient:

options.html: Blood cultures, 2nd large bore IV, NS bolus 1 L IV, urine culture, piperacillin-tazobactam IV
Blood cultures, NS bolus 1L IV, urine culture, ampicillin IV
Blood cultures, Ringer's lactate 1 L IV, urine culture, metronidazole IV
Blood cultures, 2nd large bore IV, Ringer's lactate 500 cc IV, urine culture, lumbar puncture, azithromycin IV
Blood cultures, oral fluid challenge, urine culture, ciprofloxacin PO

answer: The correct answer is A. A; The patient has signs suggestive of sepsis (hypotension and tachypnea) in the setting of infection. The symptoms suggest a potential urinary tract source. Treatment of poor perfusion should be with 2 large bore IVs and at least 1L crystalloid bolus (NS or Ringer's). It is prudent to start broad spectrum parenteral antibiotics such as piperacillin-tazobactam, ideally after obtaining blood cultures and a urine culture. Ampicillin, metronidazole and azithromycin are parenteral antibiotics, but not broad enough coverage, and have incomplete coverage of urinary pathogens as well. Oral fluids and antibiotics are not the first line treatment recommendations for sepsis.

stem: A 63-year-old man presents to the ED with 2 hours of chest pain and shortness of breath. His vital signs are as follows: HR - 80, BP - 95/42, RR - 24, T - 37.1°C, O2 sat - 96%. A stat EKG is ordered and is attached. Which of the following statements is FALSE?

options.html: The EKG is diagnostic for an inferior STEMI
The EKG has evidence of reciprocal changes
The lesion is likely in the right coronary artery
Up to 3 sprays of sublingual nitroglycerine should be initiated
A 15 lead EKG should be ordered and can include the following leads: V4R, V8, V9

answer: The correct answer is D. D; The EKG is diagnostic for an inferior STEMI (ST elevation in leads II, III, aVF). There are reciprocal changes (ST depression in the lateral leads (I, aVL). The lesion is likely in the right coronary artery, as that is most common cause of inferior STEMI. A 15 lead should be ordered to assess for RV and posterior myocardial involvement. NTG spray should not be initiated as blood pressure is already on the low side, and if this patient has RV infarction, they will get profoundly hypotensive with preload reduction.

stem: You are called to assess a 75-year-old woman on the ward with a complaint of shortness of breath. She is post-operative day 7 from a debulking surgery for ovarian cancer. She has had no chest pain, nor cough or fever. On examination her vitals are: HR - 119, BP - 128/85, RR - 28, T - 36.8°C, O2 sat - 95%. Her chest is clear bilaterally and heart sounds are normal. There is no swelling, redness or tenderness in her legs. Which test is NOT indicated in this patient to help clarify the diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is E. E; The clinical findings of tachycardia, dyspnea, and normal breath sounds in a patient who is both post-operative from surgery and has cancer, all strongly point towards a diagnosis of PE. If you were to calculate her Well's Score, it would be greater than 4, so using a d-dimer would be inappropriate. A D-dimer can only be used to exclude PE in patients who are low risk for PE. A CXR, Point of Care Ultrasound (heart, lungs), EKG and CT pulmonary angiogram would all be appropriate tests to rule in/out the suspected diagnosis.

stem: A 63-year-old female presents to the ED with an 8-hour history of chest heaviness and shortness of breath. On examination his vitals are: HR - 75, BP - 100/55, RR - 30, T - 36.5 ºC, O2 sat 72% on room air. She is diaphoretic, grey and appears anxious. She is sitting in the tripod position and using accessory muscles to breath. Auscultation of the chest reveals diffuse crackles bilaterally. Heart sounds are normal. JVP is elevated. Extremities are poorly perfused, and ankles are edematous. This patient is in shock. Classify it:
answer: The correct answer is B. B; While hypotension and poor peripheral perfusion are typical of obstructive, cardiogenic and hypovolemic shock, an elevated JVP is typical for obstructive and cardiogenic shock. Pulmonary edema is more typical for cardiogenic shock. The patient also has chest heaviness, which suggests a potential cardiac etiology. Septic shock is a form of distributive shock. Distributed shock has warm, well perfused periphery due to inappropriate vasodilation.

stem: A 19-year-old male is brought to the emergency department by paramedics from home with decreased level of consciousness. He was at work earlier in the day (auto repair shop) and came home early complaining of feeling unwell. He was vomiting and complaining of flank pain. One hour later he was found unresponsive by his mother. On exam he is moaning to pain, but otherwise unresponsive. With stimulation he withdraws his arms and legs. Vitals: Heart rate 124, regular Respiratory rate 36 Oxygen saturation 100% on oxygen by mask Blood pressure 88/54 Temperature 37.4°C Laboratory: Hemoglobin 154 g/L (normal range 120 -150 g/L) White blood count: 16.2 x 109/L (normal 4 -10 x 109/L) Platelets 368 x 109/L (normal 150 -400 x 109/L) INR: 1.1 (normal 0.9 -1.1) PTT: 28 s (normal 25 -27 s) Sodium 146 (normal 135 -145 mmol/L) Potassium 4 (normal 3.5 -5.5 mmol/L) Chloride 108 (normal 98 -108 mmol/L) Bicarbonate 8 (normal 22 -29 mmol/L) Lactate 3.4 (normal 0.9 -2.4 mmol/L) Urea 13.1 (normal high 8.3 mmol/L) Creatinine 168 (normal 40 -150 mmol/L) Glucose 8.9 (normal 3.4 -8 mmol/L) Blood gases: pO2: 248 on oxygen by mask pCO2: 16 HCO3: 7 pH: 7.08 Osmolality: 340 Urinalysis: crystals seen Based on the information provided what is the most likely cause of this patient's illness?
answer: The correct answer is D. D; All of the substances listed can cause altered mental status. You should have calculated the Anion Gap and Osmolar gap and found that both are elevated. The blood gases also confirm a metabolic acidosis. All of this should lead you to consider toxic alcohols. The crystals in the urine point towards ethylene glycol specifically.

stem: A 48-year-old female presents after overdosing on her antidepressant medication. She is lethargic on arrival. Her vitals are: HR 110, BP 108/70, RR 24, O2 saturation 97% on room air, T 37°C oral Shortly after arrival she has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Post-seizure her GCS is 6, and this does not improve over the ensuing 30 minutes. An ECG is ordered that shows a wide QRS. Which is NOT indicated in this patient?
answer: The correct answer is C. C; The clinical signs in this case all point towards TCA overdose. Antidepressant medication, altered mental status, seizure, wide QRS. Treatment of TCAs is with sodium bicarb for wide QRS / wide complex tachycardia, and benzodiazepines for seizures. All patients with altered mental status / seizure should have a point of care glucose, to ensure that is not the etiology. Intubation is indicated in this patient, as she is GCS 6 despite being 30 minutes post seizure (not protecting her airway). She also has a poor predicted clinical course as patients with TCA significant TCA overdose often get worse / die. Physostigmine is not a treatment for TCA overdose. It is a cholinesterase inhibitor.

stem: A 26-year-old female is brought to the Emergency Department (ED). She was at a football game and fell 20 feet from the stands. The paramedics have started two large bore intravenous lines and have placed her in a C-spine collar. Her vital signs on arrival to the ED: pulse 126/minute, blood pressure 76/40 mm Hg, oral temperature 37.2 degrees C, respiratory rate 22/minute, oxygen saturation on a non-rebreather mask 90%, point of care glucose -8.4 mmol/L. Breath sounds are equal bilaterally, the trachea is midline and there is no jugular venous distension. Heart sounds are normal. The pelvis is stable and there is no apparent femur fracture. She has an obvious open right lower leg fracture that has been splinted. Her Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is 8. What is the most likely source of shock?
answer: The correct answer is C. C; Shock in the setting of trauma should always be hemorrhagic until proven otherwise. You cannot have enough blood loss into your head to cause hemorrhagic shock. Retroperitoneal hemorrhage is less likely than intra-abdominal hemorrhage as the pelvis is stable. Pericardial tamponade and neurogenic shock are not forms of hemorrhagic shock and are far less common/likely than hemorrhagic shock. There are also no clinical signs to specifically suggest pericardial tamponade (e.g., muffled heart sounds, jugular venous distension) or neurogenic shock (e.g., bradycardia, inappropriate vasodilation).

stem: Which of the following statements is most correct?

options.html: The absence of a gag reflex suggests an inability to protect the airway
Abnormal vital signs always indicates the need for resuscitation
Chin lift is the initial maneuver of choice to open the airway in trauma patients
A venturi mask is a good initial choice in managing a patient with severe hypoxia
When assessing patients who are pulseless, you should not begin with the ABCs (airway, breathing, circulation) but instead address the circulation first

answer: The correct answer is E. E; Many normal people have an absent gag reflex at baseline. It should not be used as a method of assessing airway protection. Abnormal vital signs do not always indicate the need for resuscitation. When you are exercising your heart rate is high, yet you do not need resuscitation. Chin lift should not be used in trauma patients, as it involves head/neck manipulation which is contraindicated in the setting of potential c-spine injury. Jaw-thrust should be used instead. A venturi mask is not used in patients with severe hypoxia as it is not the highest flow FiO2 available. You should start high, then wean as tolerated. When assessing patients who are pulseless or unresponsive, you should start with a pulse check, so you address circulation first.

stem: A 50-year-old male presents with a large area of redness and pain over his right thigh that developed over the past 48 hours. He has had a fever and feels generally unwell. He is alert and oriented. His vitals are as follows: BP 82/43 HR 135 RR 22 Temp 39.3ºC Oxygen saturation 95% on room air Does this patient have sepsis? Choose the best answer below:

options.html: Cannot determine until blood culture results are known
Cannot determine until lab results are back

answer: The correct answer is E. E; The clinical picture is consistent with a soft tissue infection. The qSOFA score for sepsis is positive for sepsis if at least 2 of the 3 clinical findings are present: 1) GCS < 15, 2), RR > or = to 22, 3) SBP < or = 100. This patient has 2 of these 3 criteria. Sepsis is a clinical diagnosis. You do not need to wait until blood cultures to come back (will take days, and are frequently negative even in presumed sepsis), or laboratory results. The SOFA score can also be used, and it does require the laboratory results to be back, but you can use the qSOFA score when laboratory results are not available.

stem: You are asked to assess a hypotensive adult patient. On examination vital signs are: HR 132, regular BP 86/48 RR 26 JVP low by clinical examination Periphery: warm with good capillary refill Temp 35.8ºC The most likely cause of shock in this patient is:
answer: The correct answer is E. E; While tachycardia, hypotension and tachypnea are clinical signs of many types of shock, the warm periphery with good capillary refill is the hallmark of distributive shock. Septic shock and neurogenic shock are both types of distributive shock. However, hypothermia (or hyperthermia) is typical of septic shock, not neurogenic shock. There is no such thing as "hypothermic shock".

stem: A 78-year-old man is admitted after a fall in the bathroom. Report from the paramedics is that he is unconscious with no response to voice, and flexion to pain on the left, extension to pain on the right. His right pupil is fixed and dilated. He is placed on a monitor; intravenous catheters are being inserted and blood work is being sent. He has noisy upper airway sounds that are improved with jaw thrust. Breath sounds are equal bilaterally, and trachea is midline. Heart sounds are normal. JVP is not visible above the sternal notch. Abdomen is slightly distended, with no guarding on examination. Vitals are: BP 104/68 HR 116 sinus RR 22 Temp 36.2ºC Oxygen saturation 85% on high flow oxygen non-rebreather mask The most appropriate next step in management is:

options.html: Emergency OR for presumed intracranial epidural hematoma

answer: The correct answer is C. C; While jaw thrust helped to open the airway, it is not protected (GCS<8) and predicted clinical course is poor (signs of brain herniation). Breathing is also concerning. Sats are poor even on high flow oxygen. This patient will also need to have a CT head, so will need to leave the monitored setting of the ED. Intubation is indicated for all of these reasons. It is not safe to have the patient leave the department without intubating first. A more detailed survey will also have to wait until ABCs have been addressed. Surgery will not be performed without imaging first to identify the type and location of bleeding. There is no current role for giving blood. While hemorrhagic shock from concomitant abdominal trauma cannot be excluded, Airway & Breathing still come before Circulation, and crystalloid would be given prior to blood.

stem: When dealing with a severely hypothermic patient, excessive mechanical jostling of a patient should be avoided because (of):

options.html: Increased regurgitation secondary to poor gastric motility
Susceptibility to hypothermia related orthopedic fractures
Hypothermic muscles are easily injured resulting in rhabdomyolysis
Increased shivering and oxygen consumption initiated by movement of the patient

answer: The correct answer is A. A; Excessive mechanical jostling should be avoided in severely hypothermic patients because it can precipitate serious cardiac dysrhythmias. The other listed answers are untrue.

stem: A 52-year-old woman is admitted with a history of three days of vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain and distension. She is cold, clammy and has decreased capillary refill, and has had 12 ml of urine output over the last hour. Her vitals are: BP 120/86 HR 114 RR 18 Temperature 38.7ºC Is she in shock?

options.html: No, because her blood pressure is normal
Cannot say without knowing her response to intravenous fluid bolus
Yes, because she has evidence of decreased perfusion
No, because urine output is adequate

answer: The correct answer is D. D; Hypotension is not a requirement to make the diagnosis of shock. Patients with evidence of poor perfusion (cold, clammy skin, decreased refill, and reduced urine output), especially in the setting known volume loss, can be presumed to have shock.

stem: In late December, a community Emergency Department receives a warning call that paramedics will be arriving in 7 minutes with a 17-year-old female who was found VSA (Vital Signs Absent) and “cold as a rock” in the woods near her house. Her driver's license led police to contact her parents who last saw her 4 hours earlier. On arrival effective CPR is being carried out by paramedics. After aggressive rewarming and resuscitative efforts, the patient's temperature rises by 1.5°C. Her serum potassium level is 6.9 mmol/L (normal range 3.5-5.0 mmol/L). Her best chance for survival would be:

options.html: Bilateral chest tubes for thoracic lavage
Call nephrology to initiate STAT hemodialysis
Continue with current rewarming and resuscitation
Futile at this point. Efforts should be discontinued since neurologic outcome appears unfavourable
Transfer to a cardiopulmonary bypass or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation capable center

answer: The correct answer is E. E; Heated irrigation (thoracic lavage) is less effective than corporeal rewarming and associated with significant complications. The most effective form of corporeal rewarming is cardiopulmonary bypass or ECMO (better than hemodialysis). CPB or ECMO is the best choice for patients with hemodynamic instability, cardiac arrest or those who fail to rewarm with less invasive active internal rewarming techniques. Termination of the resuscitation would be inappropriate as the patient has not been adequately warmed, and potassium is not > 12. A very high potassium is a poor prognostic indicator and may be suggestive that resuscitation should be terminated.

stem: The American College of Surgeons have a classification of the stages of hemorrhagic shock. Which related statement is TRUE?

options.html: It can be used to accurately and reliably predict vital sign changes in patients with a massive intracranial hemorrhage
Urine output is a useful indicator of severity in the initial assessment of patients with hemorrhagic shock
Hypotension is an indicator of stage II shock
Pulse pressure is calculated by 1/3 x (SBP-DBP) + DBP
It does not accurately and reliably predict vital sign changes in all adult patients with hemorrhagic shock

answer: The correct answer is E. E; You cannot have enough blood loss into your head to cause hemorrhagic shock. Urine output is not a useful indicator of severity in the INITIAL assessment of patients with hemorrhagic shock, as urine output needs to be measured over the period of an hour or longer. Hypotension is an indicator of stage III shock, not stage II. Pulse pressure is calculated by SBP-DBP. While this classification system is useful, it does not accurately and reliably predict vital sign changes in all patients with hemorrhagic shock. Elderly patients, or those on medications such as beta-blockers, calcium-channel blockers, etc. may not have the same clinical signs at each stage of shock.

stem: Which of the following is TRUE regarding methods of oxygen delivery?

options.html: 2L of oxygen via nasal prongs delivers an FiO2 of about 36%
A Venturi mask is an effective method for oxygen delivery in patients who are at risk for hypercarbia with uncontrolled oxygen therapy
A non-rebreather mask always delivers an FiO2 of at least 95%
A nebulizing / aerosol mask usually delivers an FiO2 of approximately 30%
Providing 8L of oxygen by nasal prongs is usually better tolerated by patients compared to using a face mask

answer: The correct answer is B. B; 2L of oxygen via nasal prongs only delivers an FiO2 of about 24%. A good guide: room air is 20-21%, then add about 4% for every 2 L via nasal prongs. A Venturi mask is an effective method for oxygen delivery in patients who are at risk of hypercarbia with uncontrolled oxygen delivery. It has an entrainment device that controls the FiO2. While a non-rebreather mask CAN deliver an FiO2 of up to 95%, it depends on the fit of the mask, and the oxygen flow rate from the tank. A nebulizing / aerosol mask usually delivers an FiO2 of about 40-60%. Providing 8L of oxygen by nasal prongs is usually not comfortable for the patients, as these high flow rates are very irritating to the nares.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the ED with a complaint of sore throat, difficulty breathing and feeling unwell for 48 hours. His GCS is 15 and he is able to speak full sentences, although his voice sounds abnormal. He looks moderately distressed, and you note audible stridor. He continually spits his oral secretions into a basin. His vital signs are as follows: HR - 122, BP - 148/92, RR - 28, T- 39.0°C, O2 sat - 98% Select the statement that is most TRUE with regards to his airway assessment.

options.html: His airway is patent as he is able to speak to you
His GCS is >8, so intubation is not indicated
His airway assessment demonstrates "problematic" features, and urgent expert assistance with airway management should be sought
His airway is patent as his oxygen saturation is normal
An oral airway should be placed immediately to manage airway obstruction

answer: The correct answer is C. C; Just because someone can speak to you, does not mean the airway is patent. He has evidence of abnormal patency with stridor, and muffled voice. Also, he cannot handle his own secretions, he has to spit them out continuously. This intubation should be assumed to be difficult and there is a need for urgent management, as the airway could completely obstruct at any moment. Getting help is prudent. Level of consciousness is not a concern, but that is only one indication for intubation. Airway patency is not assessed by oxygen saturation. That is part of your breathing assessment. If oxygenation is poor, it can be an indication for intubation.

stem: What is a clinical finding unique to distributive shock compared to other types of clinical shock?
answer: The correct answer is E. E; Distributive shock is the only type of shock that is associated with inappropriate vasodilation / normal capillary refill. Tachycardia, decreased urine output and altered mentation can be seen with any type of shock. Elevated JVP can be seen with obstructive or cardiogenic shock.

stem: A 35-year-old man collapses on arrival at the ED triage. You palpate his carotid artery and find that he is pulseless. You shout for help and for someone to go get the crash cart. Your next step should be:

options.html: Perform a head-tilt-chin-lift and deliver 2 rescue breaths
Start chest compressions at a rate of 100-120 per minute
Place the man on his side in the recovery position

answer: The correct answer is B. B; In a pulseless patient, after calling for help, the next step is to start chest compressions at a rate of 100-120/minute. Once the crash cart arrives, a rhythm check can be performed and if the patient is in VF or pulseless VT, then defibrillation should be performed. There is no role for defibrillation if the rhythm is PEA or asystole. Cardioversion is reserved for treatment of rhythms with a pulse. Rescue breathing should be performed after the first 20 chest compressions. It is not the first step. Placing the patient in the recovery position is not an appropriate course of action in pulseless patients.

stem: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding accidental hypothermia?

options.html: A core body temperature of 29°C is classified as severe hypothermia
Providing warmed humidified oxygen is an example of active external rewarming
One risk of active external rewarming is core temperature after-drop
Hypothermia is defined by a core body temperature less than 36°C

answer: The correct answer is D. D; A core body temperature of less than 28 (not 29) degrees C is classified as severe hypothermia. Standard thermometers cannot measure below 34 C. Humidified oxygen is a method of active core rewarming, not active external rewarming. Hypothermia is defined by a core body temperature less than 35 C. One risk of active external rewarming is core temperature after-drop. Cold blood from the periphery returns to the core as extremities are rewarmed, and core temperature drops further.

stem: A 69-year-old woman is brought to the ED with a chief complaint of dyspnea. She has a witnessed VF cardiac arrest and after approximately 7 minutes of resuscitation, has return of spontaneous circulation. It is now 30 minutes post cessation of CPR, and she is still unresponsive. She has been intubated and has intravenous access. Which of the following are NOT priorities for her post-arrest care?

options.html: Ventilating at a rate of 14-16 breaths/min
Maintaining a MAP of >65 mm Hg

answer: The correct answer is A. A; Maintaining a MAP of > 65, obtaining an ECG, Targeted Temperature Management and glycemic control are all post-arrest care priorities. Ventilation at a rate of 10 breaths per minute is another target. You want to avoid hyperventilation, so a rate of 14-16 is too high.

stem: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding benzodiazepine toxicity?

options.html: All patients should receive flumazenil to help reverse toxicity
Oxygen should be provided to all patients with evidence of significant sedation
Mild hypotension is an unexpected complication
Combined ingestion with ethanol is more likely to require intubation
Tachycardia is a common vital sign abnormality

answer: The correct answer is D. D; Flumazenil should not be given to all patients with benzodiazepine toxicity because it can lower the seizure threshold. It is mostly reserved for use in iatrogenic toxicity, where it can be confirmed it is the sole toxin. Oxygen should not be provided to all patients with evidence of significant sedation. Only those with inadequate breathing/oxygenation. If given to all patients, it may lead to delayed recognition of respiratory deterioration. Mild hypotension and bradycardia (not tachycardia) are typical signs of benzodiazepine overdose. When benzodiazepines are combined with ethanol, there is substantial risk of respiratory depression, and need for intubation.

stem: All of the following are indications for a definitive airway EXCEPT:
answer: The correct answer is B. B; GCS < or = 8 is an indication for a definitive airway, not < 10. The others are all potential indications for intubation.

stem: A 21-year-old male falls 3 storeys at a construction site. As part of his resuscitation, he receives 15 units of packed red blood cells. Which of the following complications would you NOT anticipate for this patient?

options.html: A platelet count of 102 x 109 (N 150-400 x 109)

answer: The correct answer is C. C; Packed cells are kept in a fridge, so rapid administration can lead to hypothermia. Massive transfusion of packed cells can cause coagulopathy from dilution of coagulation factors (high INR, low fibrinogen) and platelets (low platelet count). Hypocalcemia can occur with massive transfusion because the preservative citrate in packed cells binds calcium.

stem: A 42-year-old farmer presents to the ED after having a seizure. On examination you note that he has secretions that are frothing from his mouth, and tears draining from his eyes. His breathing is distressed, and auscultation of the chest reveals wheezes and harsh noises. The nurse comments that he has been incontinent of stool and urine. Which toxidrome has been demonstrated by this patient's presentation?
answer: The correct answer is E. E; This patient has symptoms compatible with cholinergic poisoning (salivation, lacrimation, bronchorrhea, urination, stool incontinence and seizure). This is probably due to organophosphate poisoning, which is a pesticide

stem: When considering potential causes of a PEA cardiac arrest, which of the following are NOT part of the classic “H's” and “T's” that you should include in your differential?
answer: The correct answer is A. A; Hyponatremia is not one of the classic H's and Ts included in potential causes for PEA cardiac arrest.

stem: You are treating a 73-year-old female in the ED for pneumonia. Over the next few hours her systolic blood pressure gradually trends down below 100, and her oxygen requirements and work of breathing rise. When planning her resuscitation, which of the following do you NOT need to consider?

options.html: Which Personal Protective Equipment to don
The patient's advance directive regarding resuscitation
The patient's advance directive regarding organ donation
The Power of Attorney's direction regarding resuscitation

answer: The correct answer is D. D; When planning a potential resuscitation, you should consider which PPE to don, the patient's advance directive regarding resuscitation (if there is one), whether resuscitation would likely be futile, and the POA's directives regarding resuscitation (if there is a POA). While a patient may have an advance directive regarding organ donation, physicians do not decide whether or not to resuscitate a patient based on whether or not they are willing to be an organ donor.

stem: Which of the following are typical physiological adaptations to heat stress (acclimatization)?
answer: The correct answer is A. A; Increased plasma volume is a typical physiologic adaptation to heat stress. Others include decreased heart rate, decreased sweat sodium, increased sweat volume and earlier sweating onset.

stem: You are in the hospital cafeteria when you see a man collapse. CPR is started by a nurse near the man, and you run to get the crash cart, while another person calls switchboard to activate a Code Blue. When the monitor is attached, you determine that the patient is pulseless, and the rhythm displayed is attached. What is your best NEXT step?

options.html: Wait for the Code Blue team to arrive
Transport patient immediately to the ED

answer: The correct answer is D. D; The rhythm is VT. In a pulseless patient, when the defibrillator arrives, defibrillate immediately. Do not wait until the Code Blue team arrives. A synchronized shock is cardioversion, and is only used in patients with a pulse. Transporting the patient to the ED right now is inappropriate. You don't want to interrupt CPR or defibrillation to transport a patient in cardiac arrest. It could be considered later if needed.

stem: A 28-year-old man is brought to the ED via ambulance following a high-speed car crash. He is complaining of shortness of breath, chest pain and abdominal pain. His vitals are as follows: HR –142, BP –73/42, RR –32, O2 sat 82% on non-rebreather, T –37.0 oC EMS has placed the patient in a c-spine collar. The nurse has placed the patient on a cardiorespiratory monitor. On examination you hear no stridor and voice is normal. There are diminished breath sounds on the right, and the trachea is deviated to the left. There is substantial bruising, crepitus and pain on palpation of the right hemithorax. His abdomen is diffusely tender. GCS is 14 and pupils are equal and reactive. a) What is your immediate management at this time (be specific)? You may list up to two. b) What additional area(s) of physical examination or adjunct(s) would you want in this patient (if any) as part your PRIMARY SURVEY? List up to 6.
answer: . a. This key feature question would be graded out of 1. The following would obtain 1 point: Needle decompression chest OR chest tube (1) The following would lead this to receive 0 points: Decompressing the LEFT chest Discharging the patient Sending patient outside of the ED for imaging Explanation: The clinical presentation is consistent with a right tension pneumothorax. This should be treated by decompression of the right thorax with needle and/or chest tube. Sending the patient home or sending for imaging outside of the ED is dangerous. b. b) This key feature question would be graded out of 6.0. The following would obtain 1 point each: Examine thighs / long bones / femurs (1) Look for external bleeding (1) Examine pelvis OR pelvis XR (1) Abdominal exam OR Abdominal PoCUS / FAST (1) CXR or POCUS chest (1) Group and screen OR crossmatch (1) The following responses would lead this question to receive a grade of 0: Listing advanced imaging like CT or MRI Sending the patient out of the ED / home Explanation: The primary survey involves a search for life or limb threatening injuries. These should include examination of the long bones, chest, pelvis, a search for external hemorrhage and PoCUS / FAST. It should not involve sending the patient for advanced imaging like CT or MRI, as they are too unstable to leave the ED. A CXR should also be done post chest tube insertion, but this part of the question is assessing for knowledge additional causes of shock in trauma besides the tension pneumothorax.

stem: 37. A 72-year-old female is found in bed in her apartment by her building manager after not being seen for 3 days during a heat wave in July. Her apartment has no air-conditioning. She has been brought to the ED by ambulance. Her vitals are as follows: HR –121, BP –85/48, RR –22, O2 sat - 96% on room air, T –42.0oC oral The nurse as placed the patient on a cardiorespiratory monitor. She is confused (GCS = 13) and mucous membranes are dry. She denies any pain. Examination of the chest and abdomen are unremarkable. Her neck is supple and neurological examination reveals no focal findings. a) What is (are) your leading working diagnosis(es) at this time? You may list up to two. b) What is your immediate management at this time (be specific)? List as many as are appropriate.
answer: . a. This key feature question would be graded out 1 point. The following would allow the student to earn 1 point: Heat Stroke (1) Additional answers do not earn extra points. Explanation: Hyperthermia with altered mental status in the setting of heat exposure is likely heat stroke. There are alternative diagnoses, but this must be included in the top two. b. This question would be graded out of 4 points. The following would allow the student to earn 1 point each: Obtain IV access (1) IV crystalloid bolus (NS or Ringer’s lactate) (1) Start cooling (1) Obtain fingerpick glucose / point of care glucose (1) The following responses would lead this question to receive a grade of 0: Sending the patient for imaging outside of the ED Discharging the patient Explanation: This patient is in shock and needs rapid volume expansion with crystalloid. All patients with altered mental status should have a point of care glucose to exclude it as a contributing, reversible cause. Heat stroke should be treated with rapid initiation of cooling. Patients who are unstable should not be sent outside of the ED for imaging or discharged home.
